claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt in roughly equal proportions.
A conformal CeO2 layer approximately 1–2 nm thick can be deposited on the alloy surface by atomic layer deposition.
The CeO2 coating will create a continuous nanometer-scale surface layer.
The CeO2 surface layer will generate oxygen vacancies.
The coating will promote strong metal-support interactions at the alloy–ceria interface.
CeO2 provides oxygen-storage capacity.
Alloy–ceria interfacial sites will supply mobile oxygen species that readily react with CO.
Alloy–ceria interfacial sites will supply mobile oxygen species that readily react with hydrocarbons.
The redox activity of the CeO2 coating will accelerate low-temperature oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons.
Oxygen vacancies and alloy–ceria interfacial chemistry will mitigate poisoning by H2O.
Oxygen vacancies and alloy–ceria interfacial chemistry will mitigate poisoning by NO.
The CeO2 coating will stabilize the catalyst framework against degradation during thermal cycling.
Relative to the uncoated catalyst, the coated catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature and activate below 150 °C.
Relative to the uncoated catalyst, the coated catalyst will retain higher conversion efficiency in the presence of H2O and NO.
Relative to the uncoated catalyst, the coated catalyst will retain catalytic activity better after accelerated thermal aging.
Adding CeO2 will not increase the catalyst's platinum-group-metal content.
Cu–Ni systems have demonstrated low-temperature oxidation capability.
Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts have demonstrated resistance to poisoning.
The unmodified multi-principal-element catalyst does not satisfy the combined real-world automotive performance criteria.
The long-term stability of a 1–2 nm CeO2 coating on the multi-principal-element alloy under realistic cycling and poisoning conditions is unconfirmed.
